name: Kho Kho
tagline: You can pass the chase.
hook: The fastest route to a runner might be through a teammate. Seated chasers become switches in a living circuit, handing over pursuit the moment a runner changes sides.
setup: Mark a rectangle, a central lane and an end cone at each end. Divide teams equally; all but one chaser sit along the lane facing alternate sides.
steps: Send three runners into the court. One active chaser begins beyond an end cone.
Runners may change direction and cross the lane. The chaser cannot cross it or reverse direction except around an end cone.
Tap a seated teammate’s back and call “kho”; sit in their place as they begin chasing on the side they face.
Each gentle tag scores one. Tagged runners leave; send the next three when a batch is out. Recycle batches if needed.
After five minutes, swap chasing and running. Give both teams equal turns.
win: Most tags after both teams have chased wins; a tie stands.
twist: Your position and facing direction can matter more than your speed.
variation: Intro adaptation: walk through one practice chase before running.
care: Leave generous gaps between seated players; runners go around people, never over them.
ruleNote: Shorter innings and flexible team sizes; the source explains the full nine-a-side game.

sources.title: Tamil Nadu Kho Kho Association — Game explanation

name: Kabaddi · tag edition
tagline: One raider. An entire half full of trouble.
hook: A raid is a tiny heist: cross the line, collect a tag, escape. The defenders must cooperate without crowding each other, while the raider decides how much risk is enough.
setup: Mark two equal halves. Form two teams and give every player a removable tag belt. Choose a timekeeper.
steps: Teams alternate sending one raider into the other half for up to 20 seconds.
The raider tries to remove defenders’ tags, then return across the centre line.
Defenders stop the raid by removing the raider’s tag. No tackling, holding or blocking with contact.
A safe return earns one point per tag collected. Losing the tag, stepping out or running out of time earns the defence one point instead.
Return all tags after each raid; rotate raiders so everyone has a turn.
win: After equal numbers of raids, the higher total wins.
twist: Every extra target makes the journey home more dangerous.
variation: Intro adaptation: begin with one raider versus two defenders.
care: Use a timer instead of breath holding; keep tags easy to remove and leave run-off space.
ruleNote: This designed tag-belt game removes tackling, breath control, eliminations and bonus-line rules from kabaddi.

sources.title: Oak National Academy — Kabaddi rules and basic skills

name: Lagori
tagline: Break the tower. Then rebuild it under pressure.
hook: The same tower is first your target and then your responsibility. Once it falls, the neat throwing contest becomes a frantic rebuilding mission, with decoys buying precious seconds for the builders.
setup: Stack seven discs inside a centre circle. Mark a throwing line and boundaries. One team attacks; the other fields.
steps: Attackers take up to three throws total to topple the stack. If all miss, swap roles.
Once it falls, attackers scatter and try to rebuild all seven discs.
Defenders recover and pass the ball, trying to hit attackers gently below the knees. Hit players leave this round.
A complete stack plus the call “Lagori!” earns attackers one point. Putting all attackers out earns defenders one.
Reset the tower and swap roles after either result. Play six rounds.
win: Most points after equal attacking turns wins.
twist: The best throw creates the problem you now have to solve.
variation: Intro adaptation: use five discs and roll the ball to tag feet.
care: Use soft discs instead of stone or tile; no close-range throws at a builder.
ruleNote: This fixes three team attempts and alternating rounds; catches, attempts and finishes vary locally.

sources.title: Traditional Games Federation of India — Satoliya

name: Peteca
tagline: Badminton’s flight. Volleyball’s hands. Just one touch.
hook: A feathered shuttle slows dramatically after a strike. That gives you time to read its flight, but only one touch to send it back: doubles becomes a conversation about who will commit.
setup: Mark a rectangular court divided by a net. Play singles or doubles, with the net at a comfortable height.
steps: Serve by striking the peteca with one open hand from behind the baseline.
The receiving side gets one hand strike to return it over the net; no catching or teammate passes.
Landing in the opposite court earns a point. Out, a double touch or a failed return gives the other side a point.
For this short introduction, the rally winner serves next. Play to 11, winning by two; swap ends halfway.
win: First side to win two short sets wins.
twist: One touch makes every return a decision, not a setup pass.
variation: Cooperative adaptation: remove the net and count consecutive group hand strikes.
care: Use a light beginner peteca and avoid hard downward hits near faces.
ruleNote: One-touch mechanics are documented; rally scoring to 11 and winner-serves are our introductory format.

sources.title: Peteca International — Condensed rules

name: Sepak takraw
tagline: Three touches. No hands. A whole new net game.
hook: A foot becomes a setter’s hand and a knee becomes a receiving platform. The famous acrobatics are optional: a gentle three-touch rally already feels like discovering a new way to move.
setup: Create a net court for two teams of three. Use a low net and soft training ball for a first session.
steps: A teammate tosses the ball to the server, who kicks it over from a marked service spot.
Return it within three touches using feet, legs, torso or head; hands and arms cannot contact it.
One player may take more than one touch. Keep the ball airborne and stay on your side.
A grounded ball, out-ball, net contact or fourth touch gives opponents one point. Alternate the serving team after each point.
Play to 15; at 14–14, play to 17. Take a break and change ends between sets.
win: Win two sets to win the match.
twist: The three-touch pattern feels familiar; the body language is completely different.
variation: Learning adaptation: allow one bounce per side, clearly agreed before starting.
care: Start with low kicks and knee control; leave overhead kicks to coached practice.
ruleNote: Regu scoring follows the cited 2024 rules; training ball, net height and dimensions are introductory adjustments.

sources.title: Sepak Takraw Association of Canada — Regu rules

name: Kī-o-rahi
tagline: Two teams. Two entirely different ways to score.
hook: One team collects points around the outside, then tries to bank them in the middle. The other fires at a central target. The same circular field becomes two overlapping tactical worlds.
setup: Mark an outer zone, inner ring and central target zone with a barrel (tupu). Put seven pou markers outside. Two Kīoma guards stay centrally; other Kīoma stay outside. Two Taniwha play the inner ring; others stay outside.
steps: Kīoma run or pass outside, earning one pending point for each different pou touched with the ball; repeat touches add nothing.
A Kīoma carrier banks that total by carrying across the inner ring and grounding centrally. Only a scoring carrier may leave the outside, apart from the guards.
Taniwha pass into the inner ring and shoot at the tupu for one point. Kīoma guards may block or catch, without touching the barrel.
A removed carrier tag, drop, interception or out-ball hands possession to opponents at the outer edge and erases pending pou points. No passing during a Kīoma crossing.
After either side scores, opponents restart outside. Swap roles every five minutes, giving equal time in each role.
win: After equal time in each role, the higher total wins.
twist: There is no single shared goal: each side reads the field differently.
variation: Learning adaptation: practise each scoring role separately before combining them.
care: Use tag belts and a soft ball; mark a no-standing buffer around the barrel.
ruleNote: Designed teaching version: simplified zones, single-tag turnovers and alternating scoring restarts. Local ture differ; learn with Māori practitioners where possible.

sources.title: Tū Mātau Ora — Kī-o-rahi ture and information

name: Lippa
tagline: Flick it up. Hit it away. Measure in bat-lengths.
hook: The ball is a short tapered stick, and the serve is a trick: strike its end so it jumps, then hit it in mid-air. Even one clean connection feels like a small invention.
setup: Use a large, clear field and a marked hitting base. Everyone except the hitter waits behind a safety line.
steps: Place the short lippa on its base with a tapered end accessible.
Tap that end with the longer bat to lift it, then strike it away in the air.
A complete miss uses an attempt. After a valid hit, wait until it stops and measure from the base.
Score one point per whole bat-length. Retrieve only on the leader’s signal.
Give every player five attempts and add their distances.
win: Highest combined distance wins; tied players share the win.
twist: You create your own airborne ball before you can hit it.
variation: Documented variant: fielders can cancel a hit by catching; reserve this for suitable coached equipment and space.
care: Flying wood needs a very large exclusion area; use purpose-made soft training equipment for beginners.
ruleNote: This uses FIGeST’s distance-only format, with five attempts; regional fielding and scoring versions also exist.

sources.title: FIGeST — Lippa technical sheet and rules

name: Bete-ombro
tagline: Two bats, two targets, and a race between them.
hook: Two friends defend little targets at opposite ends. A successful hit gives both of them a reason to sprint. The fielders want more than an out: they want possession of the bats.
setup: Set a target inside a small base circle at each end. Two batters defend one each; two fielders bowl from behind opposite ends.
steps: A fielder bowls the soft ball towards the far target. Its batter tries to strike it away.
After a hit, batters may exchange ends while fielders retrieve. In this adaptation, each completed exchange scores one.
A grounded bat inside a base makes that batter safe. Fielders can knock over an unprotected target with the ball.
A toppled target or clean airborne catch swaps batting and fielding roles.
Continue from the new roles; announce and agree pauses before anyone leaves a base.
win: First pair to ten runs wins after completing the last exchange.
twist: The prize for good fielding is the right to become the batting team.
variation: Intro adaptation: bowl underarm along the ground for easier first hits.
care: Leave room for bat swings. No throws at runners, and no clashing bats while running.
ruleNote: This removes body-hit outs and bat-tapping during runs; catch rules and scoring vary around Brazil.

sources.title: UNICENTRO Early Childhood Education Laboratory — Bete Ombro

name: Ampe
tagline: Clap. Jump. Choose a foot. Read your opponent.
hook: This tiny rhythmic duel has no equipment and almost no waiting. You jump together, reveal a foot together, and discover whether you predicted each other or fell into the same pattern again.
setup: Face a partner with room between you. One player scores for matching feet, the other for different feet; agree which is which.
steps: Clap together to establish a shared beat.
On the beat, make a small jump and land with one foot forward.
If both chose left or both chose right, the matching player gets one point. Otherwise the different-feet player gets one.
Reset and repeat until someone reaches ten. Switch scoring roles for the next game.
For a group, rotate partners after every game and keep the rhythm going.
win: First to ten wins a game; play both scoring roles.
twist: Rock-paper-scissors becomes a whole-body rhythm.
variation: Access adaptation: stay seated and reveal a left or right hand on the beat.
care: Use soft knees and small jumps; feet never need to touch the other person.
ruleNote: This fixes matching/different scoring roles; names and tournament formats vary.

sources.title: Open University TESSA Ghana — Games and physical exercise
Omoniyi and Afrifa — Ampe exercise study, game description

name: Pilolo
tagline: A treasure hunt with a sprint finish.
hook: The search is only half the game. Once you find an object, you still have to get home. A hiding place close to the finish can be more valuable than an obvious one.
setup: Choose a leader and a bounded search area. The leader hides one large token per player while everyone waits out of sight.
steps: Gather players behind a clear start-and-finish line.
On “Pilolo!”, search the agreed area for one token.
After finding one, return across the finish line carrying it. Do not take tokens from other players.
The first returning player wins that round; let everyone finish their search.
Change the leader, hide the tokens again and start another round.
win: Play five rounds and count first finishes, or simply celebrate each round’s finder.
twist: The best search route is also an escape route.
variation: Cooperative adaptation: time how quickly the whole group brings every token home.
care: Use visible boundaries and reachable hiding spots; no roads, climbing or tiny swallowable objects.
ruleNote: The search-and-return mechanic is documented; our five-round tally and large tokens are hosting choices.

sources.title: Open University TESSA Ghana — Pilolo

name: Jianzi
tagline: A feather, a foot, and one more impossible save.
hook: The weighted feather drops differently from a ball: quick enough to demand attention, slow enough for a clever rescue. A circle becomes a shared little laboratory of ankles, knees and timing.
setup: Stand in a loose circle on level ground with a jianzi. Leave room for each player to lift a leg comfortably.
steps: Drop the shuttle towards a foot and kick it upward to begin.
Keep it airborne with feet, knees or other body parts except hands and arms.
Pass to another player whenever possible; count every successful contact aloud.
When it touches the ground, end the rally and begin again from zero with a different starter.
win: Try to beat the group’s best rally within five minutes.
twist: The score belongs to the whole circle, including whoever makes the save.
variation: Learning adaptation: allow one catch to reset control, then restart counting after the next kick.
care: Keep kicks low and upward, away from others’ faces; enlarge the circle as confidence grows.
ruleNote: This is cooperative circle kicking; competitive net shuttlecock has a separate rulebook.

sources.title: CanadaGo4Sport — Jianzi circle activity
International Shuttlecock Federation — Shuttlecock

name: Dibeke
tagline: Kick once. Make the fielders chase a whole team.
hook: A single kicker can send several teammates running between safe boxes. Fielders suddenly have many possible targets, while runners decide whether to stay safe or help create a distracting wave of movement.
setup: Mark two safe boxes at opposite ends, a halfway line and a kicking area. Split into runners and fielders; choose a roller.
steps: The roller calls a runner’s name and rolls the ball to the kicking area.
That player kicks beyond halfway and must run to the opposite safe box. Teammates may run too. Retry a miss or short kick; three failed kicks dismiss the kicker.
Fielders pass the foam ball and gently throw below runners’ knees. A hit outside a safe box puts that runner out for the innings.
Each completed crossing scores one run in this adaptation. Stop when everyone is safe or out; roll to the next runner.
Swap roles after everyone is out or five minutes. Give each team equal innings.
win: Most total crossings after equal innings wins.
twist: Teammates can flood the field to make one runner harder to stop.
variation: Gentler adaptation: use hand tags by a stationary ball-holder instead of thrown tags.
care: Use a soft ball only, with no close-range shots; safe boxes need room for the whole team.
ruleNote: Based on Dibeke’s kick-and-run structure; short equal innings and direct run totals replace the full scoring system.

sources.title: Ulwazi Programme — Dibeke

name: Flunkyball · token edition
tagline: A knocked bottle starts a race against the reset.
equipment: Plastic bottle partly filled with water
hook: One accurate throw starts two different races: one team scores while the other rebuilds the field. This version keeps Flunkyball’s frantic stop-call rhythm and swaps the usual adult drinking for tokens.
setup: Two teams face each other behind lines about five metres from a centre bottle. Give each team ten tokens and a bowl one metre behind its line.
steps: Teams alternate one throw at the bottle, rotating throwers.
When it falls, the throwing team starts a relay: one player at a time carries one token to their bowl, returns and tags the next.
The other team resets the bottle, retrieves the ball and gets everyone back behind its line.
Only then call “Stop!” No more tokens may enter the bowl; a carried token returns to the supply.
Swap throwing teams after every attempt. A miss starts no relay.
win: First team to bank all ten tokens wins after the stop call.
twist: Your target is also your opponent’s reset button.
variation: Access adaptation: pass tokens along a seated line instead of running the relay.
care: Use plastic and a soft ball; keep relay lanes behind the teams, away from the retrieval route.
ruleNote: Flunkyball is commonly an adult drinking game. Token-relay scoring here is a designed alcohol-free adaptation.

sources.title: Flunkyball Verband Dortmund — Regelwerk

name: Kubb
tagline: Knock down a block. Create tomorrow’s problem.
hook: Fallen blocks return as new targets in the middle of the court. Every successful attack changes the next turn, until one team earns a shot at the king that has been waiting all along.
setup: Mark a roughly 5 × 8 metre rectangle. Put five kubbs on each baseline and the king in the centre. Divide six batons between teammates.
steps: Throw batons underarm, end over end, at opposing kubbs. For a simple opening, give each team six throws per turn.
Before their reply, opponents toss fallen kubbs into your half; stand them where they land as field kubbs.
Clear all field kubbs before attacking baseline kubbs. If any remain, opponents may throw from the line of the surviving field kubb closest to the centre.
Re-throw an out-of-bounds field kubb once; a second miss lets opponents place it, at least a baton-length from king and boundaries.
After clearing every opposing kubb, shoot at the king from your original baseline. Toppling it early loses immediately.
win: Clear the opposing kubbs, then topple the king legally.
twist: A successful hit sends its target back into the game.
variation: Use the documented 2–4–6 baton opening when both teams know the basics.
care: Everyone stands clear of the target half; collect wooden pieces only when throwing stops.
ruleNote: Casual six-baton opening; competition opening sequences and details vary by ruleset.

sources.title: Kubb World — Game rules
USA Kubb — Rules and tips

name: Mölkky
tagline: One pin means its number. Many pins mean their count.
hook: The pins spread wider after every throw, turning a simple skittle game into a moving arithmetic puzzle. You might need the lonely twelve, or deliberately aim for two low-value pins instead.
setup: Arrange the twelve numbered pins in the set’s starting cluster. Mark a throwing line about 3.5 metres away and choose turn order.
steps: Throw the wooden throwing pin underarm to knock down numbered pins.
If exactly one falls fully, score its number. If several fall, score the number of fallen pins.
Stand them upright where they fell, so the target pattern gradually spreads.
Take turns adding scores. Going above 50 resets your total to 25; three consecutive scoreless throws eliminate you.
Keep playing until someone reaches exactly 50.
win: Exactly 50 wins. House fallback: if eliminations leave one player, they win; if none remain, share the result.
twist: Better aim can mean knocking over fewer pins.
variation: Intro adaptation: after three misses, lose five points instead of leaving the game.
care: Wait behind the throwing line and check the entire spread before each throw.
ruleNote: These are the maker’s basic rules; the no-elimination option is an adaptation.

sources.title: Mölkky Oy — Rules

name: Pétanque
tagline: A quiet little throw can completely change the picture.
hook: Every ball is both a possible point and a piece of terrain. Sometimes you roll close; sometimes you knock an opponent away. The team that is losing the current position gets to keep trying.
setup: Choose level gravel or firm ground. Play singles or pairs with three boules per player, or triples with two. Mark a shared throwing circle.
steps: Throw the small jack 6–10 metres away, then send the first boule towards it.
The other team throws until it becomes closest or uses all its boules.
Continue with whichever team is not closest. Keep both feet grounded inside the circle while throwing.
After all balls are played, only the closer team scores: one for each boule nearer than the opponent’s nearest.
The scoring team starts the next end from a circle near the previous jack.
win: First team to 13 points wins.
twist: You choose between building a better position and destroying theirs.
variation: Access adaptation: use soft indoor boules and shorter measured distances.
care: Keep people out of the landing area; metal boules are heavy even on gentle throws.
ruleNote: A basic introduction; dead-jack situations and measurement disputes are covered by the full rules.

sources.title: Federation of Pétanque USA — How to play

name: Bocce
tagline: Read the ground. Roll a better answer.
hook: A slow ball can be the boldest move on the court. Bocce rewards reading tiny slopes, using an opponent’s ball as a stop, and leaving your next teammate something useful to build on.
setup: Mark a long, narrow lane. Split eight balls equally between two teams and choose who throws the small pallino first.
steps: Roll the pallino into the far half, then roll your first ball near it.
The team farther from the pallino keeps playing until it gets closer or runs out of balls.
When one team has no balls left, the other rolls its remaining balls. Contact between balls can change the result.
At the end, the closest team scores one for each ball nearer than the opponents’ closest.
The scoring team begins the next end, reversing the direction of play.
win: First to 12 points wins this starter game.
twist: The surface is part of your strategy.
variation: Access adaptation: let a player use a rolling ramp with their chosen direction.
care: Choose balls players can control; retrieve only after the end is scored.
ruleNote: Open-bocce scoring on a casual lane; regulation courts add specific wall and foul-line rules.

sources.title: United States Bocce Federation — Open rules

name: Cornhole
tagline: Slide, block, or drop straight through.
hook: A bag in the way might be a mistake, a blockade or a ramp. Because scores cancel at the end of the round, your last throw can erase an opponent’s brilliant opening.
setup: Face two boards towards each other. Standard adult spacing is about 8.2 metres; bring them closer for beginners. Use four bags per side.
steps: Opponents alternate underarm throws at the far board until each has thrown four bags.
A bag through the hole scores three; a bag resting on the board scores one. Ground-first bags score zero and are removed.
Wait until all bags settle, then subtract the lower round score from the higher. Only the difference is added.
Throw from the other end next round; the side that scored throws first. At a tied round, keep the previous order.
win: First to 21 or more at the end of a round wins; there is no bust penalty.
twist: A last bag can turn a whole round into zero.
variation: Learning adaptation: start closer and gradually move back after successful rounds.
care: Keep the lane clear and use beanbags light enough for every player.
ruleNote: Core American Cornhole Association scoring; shortened distances are a casual adjustment.

sources.title: American Cornhole Association — Official rules

name: KanJam
tagline: Your partner is the last-metre flight controller.
hook: The throw is only the beginning. Your teammate gets a single chance to redirect the disc, turning a near miss into a hit or a glorious downward dunk. Precision and improvisation share the same point.
setup: Set two goals facing each other, normally about 15 metres apart; shorten for beginners. Each pair has one teammate at each end.
steps: Throw from behind your goal towards your partner’s goal. They may redirect once, without catching or carrying.
A deflected outside hit scores one; an unassisted outside hit scores two; a deflection inside scores three.
Partners each throw once per team turn, then the other pair takes its turn. A ground-first throw scores zero.
Reach exactly 21; if a throw would exceed it, subtract that throw’s value instead. Complete equal team turns.
An unassisted disc staying inside through the slot or top wins immediately. Otherwise, ties use equal overtime turns.
win: Exactly 21 after equal turns, or an instant-win direct entry.
twist: The best shot may need someone else to finish it.
variation: Intro adaptation: shorten the gap until each player can reach the goal comfortably.
care: Use controlled throws and open-hand deflections; keep spectators behind the goals.
ruleNote: Scoring follows KanJam’s rules; the linked guides explain complete turns, direct entries and overtime.

sources.title: KanJam — How to play
MIT Intramural Sports — Kan Jam rules

name: Ladder toss
tagline: Aim for a rung. Hope it stays there.
hook: Two balls tied together spin through the air and wrap around a rung. But a point is not safe yet: the next throw can shake your perfect landing straight back onto the grass.
setup: Stand a three-rung frame on level ground and mark a comfortable throwing line. Give each side three differently coloured bolas.
steps: Each side tosses all three bolas underarm, then the other side takes its turn.
Leave landed bolas in place until the whole round ends; knocked-off bolas no longer score.
Score one for the bottom rung, two for the middle and three for the top.
For this simple version, use no bonuses or cancellation. Add each side’s remaining points, then clear the frame.
Reach exactly 21; if your round would exceed 21, discard that round’s points. Alternate which side starts.
win: First to exactly 21 after a complete round wins; play another round if both reach it.
twist: Points can literally fall off the scoreboard.
variation: Documented bonus option: add one for all three on one rung, or one on each rung.
care: Use soft bolas, not golf balls, for younger groups; nobody stands near the frame during throws.
ruleNote: This uses the university guide’s rung values and bust rule, with explicit simple turn order and no bonuses.

sources.title: CSU Channel Islands — Basic ladder golf rules

name: Washer toss
tagline: A small ring. A smaller target. A very loud success.
hook: The satisfying part is the tiny landing zone. A gentle toss can bounce into the box or disappear into the centre cup, and one good round can cancel every point your opponent thought they had.
setup: Place two cup-in-box targets a few metres apart. Play singles or pairs, with teammates at opposite ends. Give each side three washers.
steps: Alternate tossing washers into the far box until all six have been thrown.
A washer in the centre cup scores three; elsewhere inside the box scores one. Outside scores zero.
Subtract the lower round score from the higher; only the difference is added to the leading side.
Collect washers and play back towards the other box. The side that scored starts the next round.
win: First to 21 or more at the end of a round wins.
twist: The safe one-point box surrounds the tempting three-point cup.
variation: Precision adaptation: shrink the centre cup once everyone is landing in the box.
care: Use large rubber washers for casual play and keep feet clear of the targets.
ruleNote: Box-and-cup format; washer games have many regional scores. We omit edge instant-wins, skunks and exact-21 variants.

sources.title: Gather Together Games — Washer toss

name: Golf croquet
tagline: Everyone wants the same hoop. Only one gets it.
hook: One stroke per turn makes this a patient tactical duel. You can line up your next shot, block a rival or knock their ball away, but while you prepare, someone else may simply score.
setup: Use a croquet lawn layout with six hoops. Blue and black face red and yellow. Start near corner four; review the source’s route diagram together.
steps: Take one stroke in the fixed order blue, red, black, yellow; each player controls their assigned colour or colours.
Everyone contests the same current hoop from its marked playing side.
The first ball completely through it scores one for its side. All players then contest the next hoop.
Hitting another ball gives no extra stroke. If a ball leaves the lawn, replace it on the boundary where it crossed.
Follow the numbered twelve-hoop route in the source diagram, keeping balls where they finish. If the score reaches 6–6, contest hoop three again.
win: First side to seven hoop points wins.
twist: You can move an opponent’s ball without ever earning an extra turn.
variation: Short-session adaptation: play seven contested hoops, first side to four.
care: Keep mallet swings low and wait well clear of the striker; wider hoops make an easier introduction.
ruleNote: Golf croquet, not association croquet; advanced offside and fault rules remain in the full guide.

sources.title: Croquet England — Play golf croquet

name: Disc golf
tagline: Turn the park into a course, one flight at a time.
hook: The pleasure is choosing a route: a direct throw through a gap or a gentle curve around it. Every landing becomes the start of the next problem, and a short putt can matter as much as a huge drive.
setup: Use an established course, or agree a short course of safe basket targets on permitted open ground. Pick tees and boundaries before throwing.
steps: Everyone throws from the marked tee, one at a time.
Play each next throw from where your previous disc stopped. The farthest player usually throws next.
Count every throw until the disc finishes in the basket. A target-course adaptation may instead require touching a named target.
For this starter round, an out-of-bounds throw adds one penalty; resume just inside where it last crossed out.
Record the total for the hole, then move together to the next tee.
win: Lowest total throw count across the agreed course wins.
twist: Your previous mistake becomes the next place you have to solve.
variation: Doubles adaptation: both teammates throw, choose the better landing and both continue from there.
care: Never throw towards people or animals; wait for the entire landing area to clear.
ruleNote: Core disc-golf format; use the actual course’s signs and current rules for formal rounds.

sources.title: PDGA — Description of the game
Swiss Disc Golf Association — How to play

name: Gorodki
tagline: Demolish a tiny wooden skyline.
hook: The target is a little sculpture made from five blocks. Knocking it down is not enough: every piece must leave the square. Each new shape asks for a different angle of demolition.
setup: Mark a target square and a throwing line. Build the same five-block figure for each side; use soft practice pieces and generous clear space.
steps: Take turns with two underarm baton throws at the figure.
A block counts only when it is completely outside the target square.
Leave remaining pieces where they stop. Continue until all five have cleared.
Record the throws used, rebuild for the next player or team, and repeat with the next agreed shape.
For this short game, use three figures: a straight row, a cross and a five-block well.
win: Fewest total throws across the three figures wins.
twist: A collapsed target can still refuse to leave.
variation: Documented informal option: give equal limited throws and compare blocks cleared instead.
care: Use soft equipment for introductions; traditional heavy batons require a dedicated protected throwing area.
ruleNote: A soft-equipment three-figure introduction; formal gorodki uses a prescribed series of figures and distances.

sources.title: International Gorodki Federation — Game and figures
International Gorodki Federation — Simplified rules
